question: Why is this project split into crypto.ts, manager.ts, store.ts, breach-checker.ts, sharing.ts and http/app.ts instead of being one big file?
answer_hinglish: Yeh split random nahi hai -- har file ek alag RESPONSIBILITY aur ek alag TRUST boundary cover karti hai. crypto.ts sabse neeche hai: sirf node:crypto ke primitives (scrypt, AES-256-GCM) wrap karta hai, kisi vault ya session ka pata nahi hai isko. manager.ts bich mein hai -- yeh PasswordManager class hai jo sab orchestrate karta hai: vault lifecycle, entries, sharing, revocation, idle timeout, sab yahi se driven hote hain. store.ts sirf ek async dependency define karta hai (VaultStore interface) -- disk ya network write ka abstraction, taaki kal koi real DB plug kiya ja sake bina manager.ts chhue. breach-checker.ts ek NON-CRITICAL dependency ko wrap karta hai (provider + circuit breaker + timeout), isliye alag module hai kyunki iska failure mode manager.ts ke baaki logic se bilkul different hai (kabhi throw nahi karta). sharing.ts apne mein pure crypto hai, kisi bhi vault state ko nahi jaanta. http/app.ts sabse bahar hai -- Express ka ek thin adapter, business logic nahi. Agar sab ek file mein hota, toh testing mushkil hoti (crypto ko mock karna, breach provider ko fake karna) aur ek file ka change doosri cheez tod sakta tha.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki tum ek file ko 'core vs infrastructure vs adapter' mein tod sakte ho ya nahi -- yeh basic LLD/architecture skill hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek restaurant: kitchen (core logic), supplier delivery (store), ek health-inspector ka call (breach-checker, non-critical, kabhi block nahi karta), aur waiter (http layer, bas order le kar kitchen ko deta hai, khud khana nahi banata).
how_it_works: Har module ek bounded responsibility export karta hai; manager.ts un sabko import karke compose karta hai; http/app.ts sabse upar sirf manager.ts ko call karta hai.
in_this_project: manager.ts ke top par crypto.ts, errors.ts, clock.ts, store.ts, timeout.ts, breach-checker.ts, sharing.ts, types.ts import hote hain -- yeh literal import list hi project ki layering dikhata hai.
advantages: Har module ek independent responsibility
Testing isolated hai -- crypto.test.ts crypto.ts ko alag test karta hai
Kal koi file replace ki ja sakti hai (jaise store.ts) bina baaki ko touch kiye
disadvantages: Zyada files, zyada imports to track
Beginner ko pehli baar poora flow samajhne ke liye multiple files khulni padti hain
common_mistakes: Breach-check logic ko seedha manager.ts mein likh dena
crypto.ts mein vault-specific logic daal dena
HTTP layer mein validation duplicate karna
follow_up_questions: What would change if you swapped InMemoryVaultStore for a Postgres-backed store?
Why does sharing.ts not import from manager.ts?
Which file would you touch to add a new breach-check provider?

question: Why does sharing.ts know nothing about vaults, sessions, or revocation, and how does manager.ts bridge that gap?
answer_hinglish: sharing.ts ek PURE crypto module hai -- generateSharingKeyPair, sealForRecipient, openAsRecipient, yeh teen functions bas keys aur bytes lete hain, koi sessionId ya ownerId inhe pata nahi hota. types.ts mein comment seedha likha hai: sharing.ts itself knows nothing about vaults, sessions, or revocation, it only ever produces or consumes the crypto envelope. Iska return type ShareToken hai: sirf wrappedKey aur blob. Ab revocation aur single-use ke liye ek shareId chahiye jisse ek grant track ho sake -- par woh concept sharing.ts ka kaam nahi hai, woh manager.ts ka hai. Isliye types.ts mein SharedEntryToken banaya gaya jo ShareToken ko EXTEND karta hai aur ek extra field shareId jodta hai. manager.ts ka shareEntry() method sealForRecipient() call karta hai crypto ke liye, phir apna shareId generate karke ek ShareGrant register karta hai manager-level shares Map mein. Yeh clean separation isliye zaroori hai kyunki crypto logic (RSA-OAEP + AES wrap) aur business logic (kisne kiska share banaya, kab revoke hua) do bilkul alag concerns hain -- agar mix hota, toh sharing.ts ko unit test karne ke liye fake vaults ya sessions banane padte, jo crypto correctness test karne mein noise hai.
why_needed: Crypto correctness aur business rules (revocation, single-use) ko mix karna dono ko test karna mushkil banata hai; alag rakhne se dono independently verify ho sakte hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek sealed envelope banane wali machine (sharing.ts) ko yeh pata nahi hota ki envelope kisko diya gaya, kab cancel hua -- woh sirf seal lagana jaanti hai. Tracking number assign karna aur delivery cancel karna post-office (manager.ts) ka kaam hai.
how_it_works: sealForRecipient returns { wrappedKey, blob }; manager.ts isme shareId jod kar SharedEntryToken banata hai aur ek separate ShareGrant register karta hai.
in_this_project: types.ts mein SharedEntryToken ShareToken ko extend karta hai; manager.ts::shareEntry seal karta hai aur shares Map mein grant register karta hai.
advantages: sharing.ts testable without any vault or session setup
Crypto bugs isolated from business-logic bugs
shareId ek opaque reference hai, khud se entry open nahi kar sakta
disadvantages: Thoda indirection -- SharedEntryToken ek wrapper type hai jo samajhne mein ek extra step leta hai
common_mistakes: shareId ko crypto token ke andar daal dena jisse sharing.ts ko vault state ka pata chal jaata
Revocation check sharing.ts mein likhna
follow_up_questions: What would break if shareId were part of the encrypted blob instead of the wrapper?
How does revokeShare use the shareId without touching sharing.ts?
Why is wrappedKey base64 and not a raw Buffer in the token shape?

question: Why is src/http/app.ts a thin wrapper around PasswordManager instead of reimplementing field validation or business rules?
answer_hinglish: HTTP layer ka kaam hai: request parse karo, auth check karo, PasswordManager ka method call karo, response map karo. Field-level validation (empty title, password too long, master password too short) yeh sab PasswordManager ke methods khud already karte hain -- requireString, requireMasterPassword se, aur INVALID_REQUEST throw karte hain jo app.ts mein 400 pe map ho jaata hai. Comment seedha code mein hai: field-level type checking is deliberately not duplicated here, every PasswordManager method already validates its own inputs, so a field is simply read off the body and handed straight through. bodyField() helper sirf req.body se field nikaalta hai, kuch validate nahi karta. Ek hi deliberate exception hai: POST shares redeem ka body, jiska shape library mein check nahi hota -- isliye isShareTokenShape() yahin likha gaya, taaki malformed body openAsRecipient() tak pahunch kar raw TypeError (jaise Buffer.from undefined) na de, balki clean 400 de. Yeh design choice duplicate logic se bachata hai -- agar validation dono jagah likhi hoti, toh ek jagah update karne par doosri jagah bhool jaane ka risk hota, aur yeh exactly woh bug class hai jo DRY violate karne se aati hai.
why_needed: Validation ko do jagah likhna maintenance burden aur drift ka risk banata hai -- ek jagah update ho aur doosri reh jaaye.
real_world_analogy: Ek front-desk receptionist form ke har field ko khud validate nahi karta -- woh form andar bhej deta hai, aur jo department form process karta hai woh fail karti hai agar galat ho, aur receptionist sirf woh rejection wapas deliver karta hai.
how_it_works: bodyField(req, field) sirf req.body se field padhta hai; manager method apna validation khud karta hai aur INVALID_REQUEST throw karta hai jo error handler 400 banata hai.
in_this_project: http/app.ts::bodyField koi validation nahi karta; sirf redeem route par isShareTokenShape() ek structural check karta hai kyunki library ka apna equivalent check nahi hai.
advantages: Validation ek hi jagah maintain hoti hai
HTTP layer chhota aur simple rehta hai
Business logic kabhi do baar test nahi karni padti
disadvantages: Agar koi naya caller directly PasswordManager use kare bina HTTP ke, usko bhi same error codes milte hain -- friendlier HTTP-specific message chahiye ho toh extra mapping layer chahiye
common_mistakes: HTTP layer mein apna khud ka password-length check jodna
redeem route ke liye shape check bhool jaana aur raw TypeError leak hona
follow_up_questions: What happens if the redeem body's blob field is missing entirely -- walk through the code path?
Why does createVault route not need asyncRoute() but addEntry route does?
Where would you add a new field-level rule if you needed one only for the HTTP API?

question: Looking at the actual import statements across the files, what is this project's dependency layering -- what does manager.ts depend on, and what depends on manager.ts?
answer_hinglish: manager.ts ke top par dekho: yeh crypto.ts (decrypt, deriveKey, encrypt, newSalt), errors.ts (PasswordManagerError), clock.ts (Clock, systemClock), store.ts (InMemoryVaultStore, PersistedVault, VaultStore), timeout.ts (withTimeout), breach-checker.ts (BreachChecker), sharing.ts (generateSharingKeyPair, openAsRecipient, sealForRecipient), aur types.ts import karta hai. Yeh sab leaf modules hain -- inmein se koi bhi manager.ts ko import nahi karta, saara flow ek direction mein hai: leaves upar, manager.ts beech mein jo unhe compose karta hai. Phir http/app.ts dekho -- yeh manager.ts se sirf TYPE import karta hai, import type PasswordManager from manager.js, aur errors.ts se PasswordManagerErrorCode. http/app.ts sabse bahar ki layer hai: koi bhi dusra file http/app.ts ko import nahi karta. Yeh ek clean, acyclic dependency graph banata hai: crypto, errors, clock (sabse neeche, zero internal deps) se store, timeout, breach-checker, sharing (middle) se manager.ts (hub, sab compose karta hai) se http/app.ts (outermost adapter). Interview mein yeh batana important hai kyunki yeh dikhata hai ki core library http ke bina bhi fully usable hai -- npm start na bhi chalao, sab kuch manager.ts se directly use ho sakta hai.
why_needed: Import graph padhna ek real architecture skill hai -- yeh batata hai ki code actually kaise organized hai, docs kya bolti hain uske bajaye.
real_world_analogy: Ek company org chart jaisa: niche ke individual contributors (crypto, clock) kisi ko report nahi karte, manager (manager.ts) sabko coordinate karta hai, aur external client-facing team (http layer) manager se instructions leta hai, reverse mein nahi.
how_it_works: manager.ts leaf modules import karta hai aur unhe compose karta hai; http/app.ts sirf manager.ts ka type import karta hai, koi value-level cycle nahi.
in_this_project: manager.ts ka import block lines 15-22 par; http/app.ts ka `import type { PasswordManager } from "../manager.js"`.
advantages: Core library zero coupling to HTTP or Express
Acyclic graph -- easy to reason about and test bottom-up
Each leaf module independently unit-testable
disadvantages: manager.ts is a big hub -- it is the single biggest file and knows about every other module
common_mistakes: Letting a leaf module like crypto.ts import manager.ts for convenience, creating a cycle
Importing Express types inside manager.ts
follow_up_questions: Why does http/app.ts only import PasswordManager as a type, not a value?
What would happen to this graph if sharing.ts needed to call back into manager.ts?
Which module would you extract first if this project needed a plugin system for breach providers?

question: Why is BreachChecker its own class combining breach.ts, circuit-breaker.ts and timeout.ts, instead of manager.ts calling each piece directly inside addEntry and updateEntry?
answer_hinglish: Agar manager.ts khud circuit breaker aur timeout ko wire karta, toh addEntry() aur updateEntry() dono mein woh same wiring duplicate honi padti -- aur breach-check ek bahut specific POLICY follow karta hai: never throw, timeout, error, ya open-circuit sab null mein degrade ho jaate hain. BreachChecker.check() mein yeh poora combine hota hai: breaker.run ke andar withTimeout aur isPasswordBreached chalta hai, aur bahar ek try catch jo kuch bhi throw ho usse null bana deta hai. Yeh ek COHESIVE unit hai -- iska apna constructor hai jo default provider FakeBreachProvider, default breaker, default timeout sab khud configure karta hai. Agar yeh manager.ts mein inline hota, toh har jagah jahan breach-check chahiye (addEntry, updateEntry, checkBreach standalone) woh poora try catch plus breaker plus timeout logic repeat hota. Alag class banane se ek single, testable unit milta hai jiska apna breach-checker.test.ts hai bina kisi vault ya session involve kiye. Yeh single-responsibility ka classic example hai: har dependency jo optional ya non-critical hai usko apne resilience wrapper mein isolate karo.
why_needed: Resilience logic (breaker plus timeout plus degrade-to-null) ko ek jagah centralize karna duplicate wiring aur inconsistent behavior se bachata hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek building ka fire-alarm system apna khud ka self-test aur fail-safe logic rakhta hai, har floor usko manually wire nahi karta -- woh ek shared service hai jo sabko same guarantee deta hai.
how_it_works: BreachChecker.check() breaker.run ke andar withTimeout(isPasswordBreached) chalata hai, aur koi bhi failure catch ho kar null return karta hai.
in_this_project: manager.ts::addEntry bas `this.breachChecker.check(password)` call karta hai, poora resilience wiring BreachChecker ke andar hai.
advantages: Single, testable unit for a non-critical dependency's resilience policy
manager.ts stays simple: one method call
Defaults are centralized in one constructor
disadvantages: One more file or class to understand the full picture
Hides the breaker plus timeout composition order unless you read check() directly
common_mistakes: Calling the breach provider directly from addEntry without the breaker or timeout wrapper
Letting check() throw instead of degrading to null
follow_up_questions: What happens if the circuit breaker is open and addEntry is called -- does the save still succeed?
Why does check() swallow every error with a bare catch instead of checking error type?
How would you add metrics for circuit state transitions?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: In-memory version mein ek extra abstraction layer hai -- BreachChecker ke andar kya ho raha hai samajhne ke liye teen files dekhni padti hain. Par fayda yeh hai ki manager.ts ka addEntry sirf ek line likhta hai aur poora resilience logic kahin aur isolated hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar BreachChecker na hota aur manager.ts directly provider call karta bina circuit breaker ke, toh ek slow ya down breach-check provider har addEntry ko block kar deta -- password save hi nahi hota jab tak provider respond na kare. Circuit breaker isse bachata hai: threshold failures ke baad circuit open ho jaata hai aur agli calls fast-fail ho jaati hain bina provider ko call kiye.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative hota in-project resilience libraries se CircuitBreaker import karna. README explicitly bolta hai ki yeh nahi kiya gaya kyunki har project standalone package hai -- cross-project dependency wiring ki complexity, chhote self-contained breaker likhne se zyada costly hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x scale par breach-check calls badh jaate hain, par circuit breaker ka behavior same rehta hai kyunki woh per-instance state hai. 100x scale par agar yeh multiple API server instances mein run ho, toh har instance ka apna independent circuit breaker hoga -- ek instance down provider dekh kar open ho sakta hai jabki doosra abhi closed hai, jo inconsistent lagta hai par safe hai kyunki har ek apne traffic ko khud protect kar raha hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein circuit breaker ki state ko metrics ya logging se expose karna chahiye, getCircuitState() already hai, taaki ops team dekh sake ki breach-check provider down hai. Real HIBP API call karne ke liye isPasswordBreached ka provider ek real HTTP client banega, aur rate-limiting bhi provider side add karna hoga.

question: Why do sessions and shares live in manager-wide Maps instead of being stored inside each VaultRecord?
answer_hinglish: Dono -- sessions aur shares -- VAULT CONTENT nahi hain, yeh METADATA hain ABOUT ek transaction ya ek login. Session batata hai kaun currently unlocked hai, share batata hai ek entry kisi doosre vault ko di gayi. PLAN.md mein stage 5 ka reasoning seedha likha hai: shares Map sits alongside the existing sessions map, for the same reason, this is bookkeeping about a grant, not vault content, so it never goes through VaultStore and does not survive a restart. Code mein comment bhi hai ShareGrant ke upar: manager-level bookkeeping, like Session, not vault content. Agar yeh VaultRecord ke andar hota, toh do problems aate: pehla, yeh VaultStore ke through persist hona shuru ho jaata, jabki sessions ya shares really durable nahi hone chahiye. Doosra, revokeShare() ko har vault ke andar dhoondna padta share ke liye instead of ek flat Map.get(shareId) lookup. Manager-level Map rakhne se lookup O(1) direct hai aur persistence boundary clean hai -- exactly jo durable hona chahiye (entries, salt, canary, sharing keys) VaultStore se guzarta hai, jo nahi hona chahiye (sessions, shares) wahi plain in-memory Map mein rehta hai.
why_needed: Vault content aur bookkeeping metadata ko mix karna persistence boundary ko toda deta hai aur lookup ko inefficient bana deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Bank apne vault ke andar customer ki visit log nahi rakhta -- visit log ek alag register mein hota hai, chahe vault ka asli saamaan kuch bhi ho.
how_it_works: sessions aur shares manager class ke level par Map hain; revokeShare seedha shares.get(shareId) karta hai, har vault ko walk nahi karta.
in_this_project: manager.ts mein `private readonly shares = new Map<string, ShareGrant>()` aur `private readonly sessions = new Map<string, Session>()` class-level fields hain, VaultRecord ke andar nahi.
advantages: O(1) lookup by shareId or sessionId without walking vaults
Clean persistence boundary: only real vault content goes through VaultStore
Matches the existing sessions precedent -- consistent design
disadvantages: Neither survives a process restart
A multi-instance deployment needs a shared store for this metadata
common_mistakes: Storing shares inside VaultRecord and then needing to search every vault to revoke one
Assuming shares survive a restart like entries do
follow_up_questions: What would you use in production to store sessions and shares so they survive a restart, and why not the same database as vault content?
How would revokeShare's lookup change if shares were per-vault instead of manager-wide?
Why is this the same reasoning PLAN.md gives for where sessions live?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Sessions aur shares ko separate rakhne se ek clean persistence boundary milta hai, par iska matlab yeh bhi hai ki yeh dono kabhi survive nahi karte restart ke baad -- jo ek explicit, documented limitation hai, bug nahi.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar process crash ho jaaye, toh sab active sessions aur pending shares gayab ho jaate hain -- har user ko phir se unlock karna padega, aur koi bhi unredeemed share bhi gayab ho jaayega. Vault ka actual encrypted content jo VaultStore se gaya tha safe rehta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative hota sessions aur shares ko bhi VaultStore mein persist karna -- par woh galat trade-off hai kyunki har heartbeat ek DB write ban jaata, jabki yeh purely ephemeral state hai jisse Redis jaisi fast in-memory store zyada fit hoti.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x scale par agar yeh single-process design multiple instances mein chalaya jaaye, toh sessions aur shares ko ek shared fast store mein move karna padega taaki koi bhi instance kisi bhi session ko check kar sake -- abhi yeh per-process Map hai jo horizontal scaling mein break hoga.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein sessions aur shares ko Redis mein TTL ke saath rakhna natural fit hai -- idle timeout already ek TTL-jaisa concept hai, aur Redis ki EXPIRE feature use ho sakti hai background sweep ke bina.

question: This project keeps vaults, sessions, and shares as in-process Maps inside one PasswordManager instance. What would break first if you ran this behind multiple horizontally-scaled API server instances, and how would you redesign it?
answer_hinglish: Sabse pehle yeh break hoga: agar load balancer ek request Server A ko bheje aur agla request same sessionId ke saath Server B ko, toh Server B ke paas woh sessionId hi nahi hoga -- kyunki sessions ek in-process Map hai, PasswordManager instance-specific. Yeh immediately UNKNOWN_SESSION throw karega jabki session actually valid tha, bas galat server par poocha gaya. Same problem vaults ke saath -- do servers do independent vaults Maps rakhenge, toh Server A par createVault ke baad Server B ko woh vault pata hi nahi chalega jab tak ek shared backing store na ho. README ne already yeh limitation document kiya hai: everything is in memory, one process, nothing survives a restart including the shares grant registry and session idle clocks. Redesign ke liye teen pieces chahiye: ek, VaultStore ka ek real DB-backed implementation jo saare servers share karein; do, sessions aur shares ko ek shared fast store Redis mein move karna, sticky session routing ki jagah, taaki koi bhi server kisi bhi sessionId ko resolve kar sake; teen, lockout counters aur circuit breaker state bhi per-instance se shared state mein shift karne honge, warna ek attacker Server A par lockout trigger karega par Server B par fresh attempts kar sakta hai. Yeh sab ek bade architectural change hai -- single-process assumption poore design mein bikhra hua hai, jaise claimEntryOp jaisi synchronous-claim pattern bhi single-process JS execution model par depend karti hai.
why_needed: Horizontal scaling ek standard interview follow-up hai jab bhi system in-memory state rakhta hai -- yeh assess karta hai ki candidate scaling implications samajhta hai ya nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhota dukaan jahan malik khud sab customers ko yaad rakhta hai -- jaise hi dukaan branches mein phael jaati hai, ek shared ledger chahiye hota hai taaki har branch same customer history dekh sake.
how_it_works: Shared durable store (DB) vault content ke liye, shared fast store (Redis) ephemeral session/share state ke liye, aur lockout/circuit-breaker state bhi centralized honi chahiye.
in_this_project: README ka 'Known and NOT handled' section explicitly bolta hai: everything is in memory, one process; is project mein multi-instance support implement nahi hai.
advantages: Current single-process design is simple and race-free by construction
VaultStore abstraction already exists as the seam for a real backend
disadvantages: No horizontal scalability as built
Sessions, shares, and circuit-breaker state would all need to move to a shared store
common_mistakes: Assuming sticky sessions alone fully solves scaling -- it does not fix vault data sharing
Forgetting that claimEntryOp's synchronous-JS-execution guarantee stops being true once state moves to a network-backed store
follow_up_questions: How would you make claimEntryOp's race-prevention logic work against a shared database instead of in-process flags?
What would a Redis-backed session store look like for isSessionActive and requireSession?
Would you keep the circuit breaker per-instance or make it shared -- why?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Single process design simple aur fast hai, synchronous claims, no network round-trip for a lock, par horizontal scale nahi karta. Multi-instance design zyada complex hota hai, distributed locks ya DB-level transactions chahiye, par availability aur scale deta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar sticky sessions use karke yeh problem avoid kiya jaaye, toh bhi ek server crash hone par uske saare sessions, shares aur in-flight claims gayab ho jaate hain -- users ko re-unlock karna padega, aur koi bhi pending claimEntryOp ka rotating ya pendingEntryOps state bhi gayab ho jaata hai.
advanced.alternatives: Sticky session routing ek quick-fix hai par single point of failure per user banata hai aur load balancing uneven ho sakti hai. Dusra alternative hai poora state ko Redis ya DB mein move karna aur PasswordManager ko stateless banana -- zyada kaam, par real horizontal scaling deta hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x scale par sticky sessions shayad kaam kar jaaye. 100x scale par yeh fail ho jaata hai -- hot vaults ek hi server par load concentrate karte hain, aur server crash ka blast radius bhi bada ho jaata hai. Poora redesign hi sustainable path hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein claimEntryOp jaisi synchronous-in-process claims ko database-level locking (jaise optimistic version check, jo already StoredEntry.version mein exist karta hai) se replace karna hoga. Circuit breaker state Redis mein shared karni hogi, ya per-instance rakh ke bhi accept karna ki thoda inconsistency ho sakta hai.

question: This project is fully in-memory, but if VaultStore were backed by a real database, what table(s) would you design based on the PersistedVault shape?
answer_hinglish: PersistedVault ka shape dekho: ownerId, createdAt, salt (base64 string), canary (EncryptedBlob: iv, ciphertext, authTag), entries (array of PersistedEntry: id, blob, createdAt, updatedAt, lastUsedAt), sharingPublicKey, wrappedPrivateKey. Natural mapping yeh hota: ek vaults table jisme ownerId PRIMARY KEY ho, saath salt aur canary ke columns, sharingPublicKey, wrappedPrivateKey. Phir ek alag entries table jisme har row ek entry ho, foreign key owner_id vaults table ki taraf, aur blob ke liye iv, ciphertext, authTag columns, plus createdAt, updatedAt, lastUsedAt. Entries ko alag table mein rakhna zaroori hai kyunki ek vault mein kayi entries ho sakti hain, jabki agar entries ko vaults row ke andar JSON array mein daalo, toh ek single entry update karne ke liye poora vaults row rewrite karna padta -- jo concurrency ke liye bura hai. Yeh exact wahi PersistedVault, PersistedEntry split hai jo store.ts mein already defined hai -- commit() function already is granularity par sochta hai.
why_needed: Schema design ki shuruaat hamesha existing data shape se honi chahiye, taaki tables actual access patterns reflect karein, guesswork nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek file cabinet (vaults) aur uske andar ek drawer (entries) alag rakho -- taaki ek drawer khulne se poora cabinet uthana na pade.
how_it_works: PersistedVault ke top-level fields vaults table banate hain; entries array ek separate entries table banata hai with a foreign key.
in_this_project: store.ts::PersistedVault aur PersistedEntry interfaces exactly yeh schema design dictate karte hain.
code_example:
-- illustrative, not from the repo (this project has no real DB) -- based on PersistedVault/PersistedEntry
CREATE TABLE vaults (
  owner_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at BIGINT NOT NULL,
  salt TEXT NOT NULL,
  canary_iv TEXT NOT NULL,
  canary_ciphertext TEXT NOT NULL,
  canary_auth_tag TEXT NOT NULL,
  sharing_public_key TEXT,
  wrapped_private_key_iv TEXT,
  wrapped_private_key_ciphertext TEXT,
  wrapped_private_key_auth_tag TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE entries (
  id TEXT NOT NULL,
  owner_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES vaults(owner_id),
  iv TEXT NOT NULL,
  ciphertext TEXT NOT NULL,
  auth_tag TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at BIGINT NOT NULL,
  updated_at BIGINT NOT NULL,
  last_used_at BIGINT,
  PRIMARY KEY (owner_id, id)
);
advantages: Entries table allows per-entry updates without rewriting the whole vault row
Matches the existing PersistedVault/PersistedEntry split one-to-one
disadvantages: Two tables instead of one JSON blob means a join to read a full vault
common_mistakes: Putting entries as a JSON array column on vaults, making single-entry updates expensive
Forgetting owner_id foreign key on entries
follow_up_questions: Why would you NOT store entries as a JSON array on the vaults row?
What happens to this schema if a vault needs to support more than one owner later?
How would the version field, used for ENTRY_CONFLICT, fit into the entries table?

question: Why does PersistedVault persist salt and canary but never the master password itself, and what would those columns look like in a vaults table?
answer_hinglish: Master password KABHI persist nahi hota -- na plaintext, na hash. Jo persist hota hai woh hai salt (ek random 16-byte value, newSalt se banta hai) aur canary (ek EncryptedBlob, fixed plaintext jo master-password-derived key se encrypt hua hota hai). manager.ts ka createVault() exactly yeh karta hai: salt newSalt se banta hai, key deriveKey(masterPassword, salt) se, canary encrypt(key, CANARY_PLAINTEXT) se. Verification ke time, verifyMasterPassword mein candidate password se key derive hoti hai same salt ke saath, aur canary decrypt karne ki koshish hoti hai -- AES-GCM ka auth tag khud bata deta hai key sahi thi ya galat, bina kisi separate comparison ke. DB mein yeh columns honge: salt text, canary_iv, canary_ciphertext, canary_auth_tag. Important baat: na toh salt na canary SECRET hain -- yeh dono bina master password ke kisi ko kuch nahi batate, isliye plain columns mein rehna fine hai. Agar koi hash column bhi add karta, toh woh ek dusra secret hota jo salt aur canary se SYNC rehna padta -- isliye yeh project deliberately ek hi KDF artifact use karta hai, do nahi.
why_needed: Do independent secrets (hash aur canary) rakhna sync-drift ka risk banata hai; ek hi verification artifact simpler aur safer hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek locker ka combination khud kahin likha hua nahi hota -- bas ek 'test item' andar rakha hota hai jo sirf sahi combination se open hota hai, woh hi proof hai.
how_it_works: createVault salt aur canary generate karta hai; verifyMasterPassword candidate key se canary decrypt karne ki koshish karta hai, fail hone par INVALID_MASTER_PASSWORD.
in_this_project: manager.ts::CANARY_PLAINTEXT ek fixed buffer hai; createVault aur verifyMasterPassword dono isko use karte hain canary banane aur check karne ke liye.
advantages: No separate password hash to keep in sync with the KDF
Salt and canary are safe to store in the clear -- they reveal nothing without the real password
disadvantages: Verifying a password always costs a full scrypt derive -- no cheap hash comparison shortcut
common_mistakes: Storing a bcrypt hash of the master password alongside the canary, duplicating the verification mechanism
Treating the salt as a secret and trying to encrypt it when it does not need to be
follow_up_questions: What would happen if an attacker read the salt and canary from the database directly?
Why is scrypt chosen over a fast hash like SHA-256 for deriveKey?
What breaks if two vaults accidentally shared the same salt?

question: Why is each entry stored as one AES-256-GCM blob covering title, username, password, and notes together, rather than four separately-encrypted columns, and how does that shape the entries table?
answer_hinglish: README ke design choices mein seedha likha hai: a single encrypted blob per entry instead of separately-encrypted fields, there is no requirement to search or sort by title or username without unlocking first, so there is nothing to gain from splitting it, and splitting it would mean more IVs and more ciphertexts to keep in sync on every write. Matlab agar title, username, password, notes alag-alag encrypt hote, toh har entry ke 4 IVs, 4 ciphertexts, 4 auth tags rakhne padte, aur updateEntry jaisi operation mein sabko ek saath consistently update karna padta. Is project mein koi feature nahi hai jo bole title ko unlock kiye bina search karo -- har access session ke through hota hai jisme key already available hai. Isliye entries table mein ek hi row har entry ke liye hoti: id, owner_id, aur blob ke teen fields iv, ciphertext, authTag jisme JSON.stringify of title, username, password, notes, breached encrypted hota hai -- exactly jaise StoredEntry.blob manager.ts mein hai. Yeh column count kam karta hai aur writes atomic banata hai.
why_needed: Zyada ciphertexts matlab zyada jagah sync out of order hone ki, aur bina real requirement ke splitting karna unnecessary complexity hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek sealed envelope mein poora letter daalna, alag-alag paragraphs ko alag envelopes mein daalne se behtar hai jab tak kisi ko ek paragraph alag se dekhne ki zaroorat na ho.
how_it_works: addEntry poora DecryptedEntryBody JSON.stringify karke ek hi encrypt() call se blob banata hai; updateEntry bhi poora merged body ek naye blob mein daalta hai.
in_this_project: manager.ts::StoredEntry.blob ek EncryptedBlob hai jo poore body ko cover karta hai, store.ts::PersistedEntry.blob isi shape ko persist karta hai.
advantages: One IV, ciphertext, authTag per entry instead of four -- fewer places to get out of sync
A single atomic re-encrypt on update, not four coordinated ones
disadvantages: Cannot search or sort by title or username at the database level without decrypting every row first
Cannot selectively re-encrypt just the password field; the whole blob is rewritten
common_mistakes: Splitting fields into separate ciphertexts for future flexibility with no actual requirement for it
Forgetting that breached is also inside the blob, not a plain column
follow_up_questions: If the product later needed to search entries by title without unlocking, what would you change?
Why is breached stored inside the encrypted blob rather than as a plain boolean column?
What is the cost of re-encrypting the whole blob on a single-field patch like updateEntry?

question: Given how entries, shares and sessions are looked up in manager.ts, what indexes would a real database backend for this project need?
answer_hinglish: manager.ts ke lookup patterns dekho: requireVault(ownerId) seedha vaults.get(ownerId) hai -- isliye vaults table mein owner_id PRIMARY KEY hona chahiye. requireEntry(record, entryId) ek entry ko uske vault ke andar id se dhoondta hai -- entries table mein owner_id aur id composite primary key ya kam se kam owner_id par index chahiye, kyunki listEntries() saare entries EK owner_id ke liye fetch karta hai. revokeShare() shares.get(shareId) karta hai aur phir share.ownerId check karta hai -- isliye shares table mein share_id PRIMARY KEY, aur ownership check ke liye owner_id ek column. Sessions table mein session_id PRIMARY KEY chahiye, kyunki requireSession() hamesha sessionId se direct lookup karta hai. Koi bhi query jo ek owner ke saare sessions dhoonde, jaise toSummary ka activeSessions count, usko owner_id par index chahiye sessions table mein bhi. Summary: vaults owner_id PK, entries owner_id plus id composite PK plus index on owner_id, shares share_id PK plus index on owner_id, sessions session_id PK plus index on owner_id.
why_needed: Index design query patterns se derive hona chahiye, guesswork se nahi -- har lookup ka ek matching index hona chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek library catalog jo book title se search allow karta hai woh title par index rakhta hai; jo author se search karta hai woh author par -- index exactly us query ko match karta hai jo actually chalegi.
how_it_works: Har manager.ts method ka lookup pattern (Map.get by key) seedha ek DB index ki zaroorat batata hai.
in_this_project: manager.ts::requireVault, requireEntry, revokeShare sab direct key-based lookups hain jo unke corresponding tables ke primary keys/indexes define karte hain.
advantages: Every index maps to an actual lookup pattern already present in the code, not a guess
owner_id index on entries directly supports listEntries' scan
disadvantages: Extra indexes cost write performance on every insert or update
common_mistakes: Indexing entries only by id, missing that listEntries needs an owner_id scan
Forgetting the owner_id index on shares needed for revokeShare's ownership check
follow_up_questions: Why does entries need a composite key instead of just id as primary key?
How would you index entries if the product later needed full-text search on titles?
What would the activeSessions count query look like with this schema?

question: Why does commit()'s snapshot include sharingPublicKey and wrappedPrivateKey alongside salt, canary, and entries, and what does that imply about which database columns must change together in one transaction?
answer_hinglish: commit() method ka signature dekho: fields argument mein salt, canary, entries, sharingPublicKey, wrappedPrivateKey SAARE explicitly pass hote hain, aur snapshot (PersistedVault) unhi se banta hai. Yeh matlab yeh hai ki PersistedVault ek ATOMIC UNIT hai -- jab bhi vault ka koi bhi state change hota hai, naya entry, update, rotation, ya naya sharing keypair, poora snapshot ek saath persist hota hai, partial nahi. Kyun zaroori hai yeh? changeMasterPassword() dekho: yeh salt, canary, entries sab re-encrypted, AUR wrappedPrivateKey re-wrapped -- sab EK commit() call mein jaata hai. Agar yeh alag-alag transactions mein hota, toh beech mein crash hone se ek INCONSISTENT state ban sakta tha -- jaise entries naye key se encrypted, par wrappedPrivateKey abhi bhi old key ke under. Real DB mein yeh ek SINGLE transaction honi chahiye jo vaults row update kare AUR entries rows ko replace kare ek saath. README ka mutation check S22 exactly isi gap ko catch karta hai: the snapshot handed to the store for that same commit could have used the OLD salt and canary.
why_needed: Multi-field state change ko partial transactions mein todna crash-time inconsistency ka direct risk hai.
real_world_analogy: Bank account number change karte waqt naya number aur naya PIN dono ek saath update hone chahiye, beech mein crash hone se account ek hybrid state mein nahi reh sakta.
how_it_works: commit() ek explicit fields object se PersistedVault snapshot banata hai aur ek single store.persist() call karta hai.
in_this_project: manager.ts::commit ke fields parameter mein salt, canary, entries, sharingPublicKey, wrappedPrivateKey sab explicitly aate hain, changeMasterPassword inhi sab ko ek call mein pass karta hai.
advantages: One atomic write means no partially-rotated vault is ever possible
Explicit fields argument prevents reading a stale value off record by accident
disadvantages: Every commit rewrites the entire snapshot even for a one-field change
A real DB needs an explicit multi-table transaction to replicate this atomicity
common_mistakes: Splitting the rotation into separate updates for salt/canary and entries, risking an inconsistent crash state
Reading record.salt directly inside commit() instead of the passed fields.salt
follow_up_questions: What isolation level would you use for the real-DB transaction that replaces commit()?
Why does commit() take fields explicitly instead of reading them off record?
How would you avoid rewriting every entry row on a single-entry update in a real DB?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: In-memory version mein atomicity free hai, ek JS object pass ho jaata hai, aur record ki fields sirf commit() succeed hone ke baad reassign hoti hain. Real DB mein yeh ek explicit transaction boundary maangta hai -- jyada code, par same guarantee.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar commit non-atomic hota, jaise salt or canary update ek transaction mein, entries dusre mein, aur beech mein process crash ho jaaye, toh vault ek corrupt state mein reh jaata -- entries naye key se encrypted hain par canary abhi purani key verify karega. Yahi bug README ke S22 mutation check ne pakda tha.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative hota entries ko salt or canary se separate transactionally commit karna with a version column linking them, par woh complexity add karta hai bina real benefit ke -- single transaction simpler hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x scale par bade vaults, hazaron entries, ke liye ek single transaction mein saari entries rewrite karna slow ho sakta hai -- production mein sirf CHANGED entries update karna better hota.
advanced.production_improvements: Production DB mein yeh poora commit() ek wrapping transaction mein hona chahiye with proper isolation level, aur agar entries bahut bade hain, batch inserts or updates use karna chahiye performance ke liye.

question: manager.ts's commit() only reassigns record's in-memory fields after persist() resolves, guaranteeing atomicity in memory. What transaction boundary would a real relational database need to guarantee the same thing, and what was the real risk the S22 mutation check exposed?
answer_hinglish: In-memory guarantee simple hai: await this.commit(...) ke baad hi record.salt, record.canary, record.entries set hote hain. Agar commit() throw kare, jaise STORE_TIMEOUT, toh yeh assignments kabhi chalti hi nahi -- record untouched reh jaata hai. Real DB mein yahi guarantee ek EXPLICIT transaction se aata hai: BEGIN TRANSACTION, vaults row update karo, entries ko delete aur re-insert karo, phir COMMIT -- agar koi bhi step fail ho, ROLLBACK hona chahiye, poora vault untouched. README ka S22 mutation yeh dikhata hai ki yeh guarantee kitni fragile ho sakti hai: commit() ko hand kiya gaya snapshot galti se OLD salt or canary use kar sakta tha jabki in-memory record pehle se NEW values rakhta tha. Is case mein koi existing test ne kabhi store mein actually kya durably saved hua check nahi kiya tha -- sirf in-memory result check hota tha. Agar commit ke beech crash hota, toh vault permanently unreadable ho jaata -- entries naye key se encrypted hote par canary purani key verify karta. Fix ek naya test tha jo store.lastPersisted(ownerId) seedha inspect karta hai aur live vault se compare karta hai.
why_needed: In-memory success ko hi 'correctly persisted' maan lena ek real-world blind spot hai -- durable store ko directly verify karna hi asli correctness check hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier ne delivery confirmation diya, par warehouse se seedha verify karna chahiye ki saamaan actually sahi address par pahuncha, sirf courier ki receipt par trust nahi karna chahiye.
how_it_works: commit() build karta hai ek snapshot aur persist karta hai; record ki fields sirf uske successful resolve hone ke baad reassign hoti hain.
in_this_project: README's mutation checks table mein S22: 'the snapshot handed to the store for that same commit could have used the OLD salt/canary.' Closed with a test reading store's lastPersisted directly.
advantages: In-memory version gets atomicity for free from JS's execution model
The real-DB equivalent is a well-understood, standard transaction pattern
disadvantages: A real DB transaction holds locks for longer on a big vault rewrite
Testing this correctly requires inspecting the durable store directly, not just in-memory state, as S22 showed
common_mistakes: Trusting only the in-memory result after a commit instead of checking what was actually persisted
Splitting the rotation across multiple non-transactional writes
follow_up_questions: How would you write a test against a real DB that reproduces what the S22 mutation check found?
What isolation level prevents another transaction from reading a half-committed rotation?
Would you use optimistic or pessimistic locking for the rotation's transaction?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: In-memory atomicity sirf JS ke single-threaded execution par depend karti hai -- koi explicit transaction primitive nahi chahiye. DB mein yeh explicit BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK chahiye, jo extra latency aur lock-holding time add karta hai par same safety deta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Bina proper transaction boundary ke, ek crash beech mein vault ko ek unreadable state mein chhod sakta hai: naya canary save hua par purani entries, ya naya entries save hue par purana canary -- dono case mein unlock() kabhi succeed nahi karega kisi bhi password se.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative approach hota saga pattern ya two-phase commit agar entries aur vault metadata alag services mein hote -- par is scale ke liye ek single-DB transaction kaafi hai, extra complexity ki zaroorat nahi.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x ya 100x scale par bhi yeh same transaction pattern chalega, bas entries ka batch size badh jaayega -- bade vaults ke liye transaction thoda lamba hoga, jo lock contention badha sakta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein ek dedicated integration test chahiye jo exactly README ke S22 jaisa check kare -- commit ke baad store se directly read karke verify karo ki persisted state live state se match karta hai.

question: Design the full real-world schema for this password manager -- vaults, entries, shares, and sessions -- and explain why shares and sessions should NOT live in the same durable store as vault content.
answer_hinglish: Poora schema char tables mein socho: vaults, owner_id PK, created_at, salt, canary iv ciphertext authTag, sharing_public_key, wrapped_private_key iv ciphertext authTag, generation int. entries, composite PK owner_id plus id, blob iv ciphertext authTag, created_at, updated_at, last_used_at, version int for ENTRY_CONFLICT. sessions, session_id PK, owner_id, generation, last_activity_at. shares, share_id PK, owner_id, revoked bool, redeemed_at nullable timestamp. Ab asli sawal: sessions aur shares ko SAME durable DB mein kyun nahi rakhna chahiye jahan vaults aur entries hain? PLAN.md ka reasoning: this is bookkeeping about a grant, not vault content. Sessions aur shares EPHEMERAL hain -- unka lifecycle minutes-to-hours ka hota hai, jabki entries aur vaults YEARS tak rehte hain. Agar dono same durable DB mein ho, toh har session heartbeat ek DB write ban jaata -- bahut zyada write load ek slow-changing table ke adjacent. Sahi design: vaults aur entries ek RELATIONAL DB mein for durability aur ACID transactions, aur sessions aur shares ek FAST key-value store Redis mein jahan TTL native support hai -- idle timeout ko Redis EXPIRE se map kiya ja sakta hai bina koi background sweep likhe. Yeh exactly wahi separation hai jo in-memory version mein already hai: vaults aur entries VaultStore se guzarte hain, sessions aur shares plain Maps mein hain.
why_needed: Different data ka different lifecycle (ephemeral vs durable) ek hi storage engine mein mix karna workload mismatch aur performance degrade karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek hotel ka permanent property records (vault content jaisa) ek secure vault mein, par aaj kaun kaun check-in hai woh ek fast front-desk whiteboard par rakha jaata hai, dono alag systems hain.
how_it_works: Durable relational DB vaults/entries ke liye ACID transactions deta hai; fast key-value store sessions/shares ke liye native TTL expiry deta hai.
in_this_project: manager.ts mein already yeh separation hai -- VaultStore (durable-worthy) vs plain sessions/shares Maps (ephemeral), jo PLAN.md ke stage 5 reasoning se match karta hai.
code_example:
-- illustrative full schema sketch
CREATE TABLE vaults (
  owner_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, created_at BIGINT NOT NULL, salt TEXT NOT NULL,
  canary_iv TEXT NOT NULL, canary_ciphertext TEXT NOT NULL, canary_auth_tag TEXT NOT NULL,
  sharing_public_key TEXT, wrapped_private_key_iv TEXT, wrapped_private_key_ciphertext TEXT,
  wrapped_private_key_auth_tag TEXT, generation INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE TABLE entries (
  owner_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES vaults(owner_id), id TEXT NOT NULL,
  iv TEXT NOT NULL, ciphertext TEXT NOT NULL, auth_tag TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at BIGINT NOT NULL, updated_at BIGINT NOT NULL, last_used_at BIGINT, version INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (owner_id, id)
);
-- sessions and shares: Redis, not this database -- see answer for why
-- sessions:{sessionId} -> {ownerId, generation, lastActivityAt} with a TTL
-- shares:{shareId} -> {ownerId, revoked, redeemedAt} with a TTL
advantages: Matches each table's access pattern to the right storage engine
Ephemeral state gets native TTL expiry instead of a background sweep
disadvantages: Two storage systems to operate instead of one
Cross-store consistency, like a session's captured generation vs the vault's current generation, requires careful application-level checks
common_mistakes: Putting sessions in the same durable table as entries and treating them as equally critical data
Forgetting shares need the same don't-leak-existence property for both missing and not-yours shareIds at the schema/query level too
follow_up_questions: How would requireSession's generation check work against a Redis-backed session?
What happens to the idle-timeout TTL if the session is touched right at the boundary?
Would you replicate the shares table's revoked and redeemedAt fields in Redis differently?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Ek single DB mein sab rakhna operationally simpler hota, ek hi backup/migration story, par write-heavy ephemeral data ko durable, slower-write DB ke saath mix karna performance trade-off hai. Dual-store approach operational complexity badhata hai par har workload ko uske sahi tool ke saath match karta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar sessions or shares bhi vault ki tarah strongly durable ho jaayein, toh normal operation mein latency badh jaati, kyunki har activity touch ek durable write ban jaata.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative: sab kuch ek hi Postgres mein, par sessions or shares tables ko UNLOGGED banake, crash-unsafe but fast -- partial middle ground, par Redis jaisa TTL-native expiry nahi milta.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x scale par session churn bahut high-frequency operation ban jaata hai -- Redis jaisa store isko easily handle karta hai horizontal sharding ke saath, jabki ek relational DB par yeh same load table bloat aur lock contention create karega.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein Redis ko sessions aur shares ke liye, aur Postgres jaisa engine ko vaults aur entries ke liye use karna, with a clear operational boundary: Redis data loss acceptable, Postgres data loss NOT acceptable.

question: What does crypto.ts's encrypt(key, plaintext) function actually do, line by line?
answer_hinglish: encrypt() function teen steps mein kaam karta hai. Pehla: randomBytes(IV_LENGTH) se har call par ek FRESH random 12-byte IV banta hai, IV_LENGTH 12 hai, GCM ke liye standard recommended length. Yeh important hai kyunki same key ke saath IV repeat karna AES-GCM todne ka sabse asaan tareeka hai. Dusra: createCipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv) se Node ka built-in cipher object banta hai with algorithm aes-256-gcm. Phir cipher.update(plaintext) aur cipher.final() ko Buffer.concat karke actual ciphertext milta hai. Teesra: cipher.getAuthTag() -- GCM mode mein encryption ke baad ek authentication tag generate hota hai jo baad mein decrypt ke time verify hota hai, yeh prove karta hai ki data tamper nahi hua. Function return karta hai ek EncryptedBlob object: iv, ciphertext, authTag sab base64 strings mein. Yeh function manager.ts mein HAR jagah use hota hai jahan bhi kuch encrypt karna ho: canary banane ke liye, entry body encrypt karne ke liye, private key wrap karne ke liye -- hamesha ek fresh IV, hamesha ek authTag, consistent pattern.
why_needed: encrypt() poore project ka foundation hai -- har secret jo kahin bhi stored hota hai, isi function se guzarta hai, isliye iska exact behavior interview mein line-by-line samajhna zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Har baar ek naya, unique lock pick karne se pehle ek naya tamper-evident seal lagana -- har baar alag seal (IV) use karna, poora confidence deta hai ki purane seal ka pattern repeat nahi ho raha.
how_it_works: Fresh IV generate, cipher create, update+final se ciphertext, getAuthTag se authTag, sab base64 mein return.
in_this_project: crypto.ts::encrypt exactly yeh steps follow karta hai; manager.ts ke createVault, addEntry, updateEntry, changeMasterPassword, getSharingPublicKey sab isko call karte hain.
advantages: Fresh IV every call eliminates IV-reuse risk automatically
Returns a self-describing blob -- iv, ciphertext and authTag travel together
disadvantages: Caller must remember to pass the right key every time -- the function itself cannot verify key correctness
common_mistakes: Reusing a fixed IV across calls -- the K2 mutation check in README specifically targets this
Storing ciphertext without the authTag, making decryption impossible
follow_up_questions: What would happen to security if IV_LENGTH were reduced to, say, 4 bytes?
Why is the IV not secret but still essential to store alongside the ciphertext?
What test in crypto.test.ts proves a fresh IV is generated every call?

question: What does crypto.ts's decrypt(key, blob) do, and why does a wrong key make it throw PasswordManagerError('DECRYPTION_FAILED', ...) instead of returning garbled plaintext?
answer_hinglish: decrypt() pehle blob ke teen base64 strings, iv, ciphertext, authTag, ko wapas Buffer mein convert karta hai. Phir createDecipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv) se decipher banta hai, aur decipher.setAuthTag(authTag) se expected auth tag set hota hai. Asli kaam try block ke andar hai: decipher.update(ciphertext) aur decipher.final() -- yahi woh jagah hai jahan GCM apna authentication check karta hai. GCM mode mein final() call khud verify karta hai ki jo authTag diya gaya woh current key, iv, ciphertext ke saath match karta hai ya nahi. Agar key galat hai, ya ciphertext ya iv ya authTag mein se koi bhi tamper hua hai, toh final() ek exception throw karta hai -- Node yeh automatically karta hai, humein manually comparison nahi likhna padta. catch block mein yeh exception pakda jaata hai aur ek clean PasswordManagerError DECRYPTION_FAILED throw hota hai. Yeh crucial hai kyunki agar GCM silently corrupted plaintext return karta, toh manager.ts ka JSON.parse(decrypt(...).toString()) ek confusing crash deta, ya worse, corrupted data ko valid treat kar leta. Authenticated encryption ka yeh exact property hi master-password verification ka pura mechanism hai -- canary decrypt karna fail ho jaana hi wrong password ka signal hai.
why_needed: Authenticated decryption samajhna crucial hai kyunki yahi property poore project ka master-password verification bina kisi separate hash ke possible banati hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek tamper-evident seal jo khud bata deti hai agar koi usko todne ki koshish kare -- sirf ek 'khul gaya ya nahi' signal, koi half-opened garbage result nahi.
how_it_works: setAuthTag + final() GCM ka authentication check karte hain; fail hone par exception, jo catch ho kar DECRYPTION_FAILED ban jaata hai.
in_this_project: crypto.ts::decrypt ko manager.ts ki verifyMasterPassword use karti hai canary check karne ke liye -- fail hona hi INVALID_MASTER_PASSWORD ka signal hai.
advantages: No manual comparison logic needed -- GCM's own final() call does the authentication check
One error code covers wrong key and tampering identically, which is the correct behavior
disadvantages: The caught error loses the specific underlying reason -- useful for security, but makes debugging a genuine corruption bug harder
common_mistakes: Never checking the auth tag at all, returning whatever bytes come out -- the K3 mutation check in README targets exactly this
Trying to distinguish wrong key from tampered data in the error message, which would leak information
follow_up_questions: How does manager.ts's unlock() use this exact throw/catch to detect a wrong master password?
Why is it correct that decrypt() cannot tell you WHY authentication failed?
What test in crypto.test.ts specifically tampers with the authTag and expects a throw?

question: Walk through manager.ts's private claimEntryOp(record) method -- what exactly does it check, what does it mutate, and why must it run with zero awaits before it?
answer_hinglish: claimEntryOp() sirf do lines ka function hai, par iska poora job hai race prevention. Pehli line: if record.rotating throw VAULT_BUSY -- agar is vault par abhi ek changeMasterPassword commit chal rahi hai, toh naya entry operation yahin reject ho jaata hai, synchronously, bina kisi store call ke. Doosri line: record.pendingEntryOps++ -- counter badhta hai jo batata hai kitne entry operations abhi in-flight hain. Yeh function kisi bhi addEntry, updateEntry, deleteEntry, getSharingPublicKey ke SHURU mein call hota hai, aur crucially, JAVASCRIPT MEIN KOI AWAIT ISSE PEHLE NAHI HOTA. Kyun important hai yeh? JS single-threaded hai aur synchronous code kabhi preempt nahi hota -- matlab do concurrent addEntry calls agar dono claimEntryOp() ko ek hi tick mein call karein, toh dono ek sequence mein chalengi, interleave nahi hongi beech mein. Isliye agar yeh check EK await ke baad hota, jaise breach-check await karne ke baad, toh do calls dono await se wapas aane ke beech mein rotating ko dekh kar dono pass ho sakte the -- jo exact race hai jo yeh rokna chahta hai. addEntry() mein dekho: breachCheck shuru hota hai, await nahi hota, phir validation hota hai, aur SIRF US SAB KE BAAD claimEntryOp() call hota hai -- still before the first real await.
why_needed: Yeh exact function race-prevention ka core mechanism hai jo stage 2 ka pura purpose hai -- iska line-by-line samajhna concurrency correctness samajhne ke liye zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek single bouncer jo ek chhoti si window mein instant decision leta hai, entry allow ya reject -- koi doosra bouncer uski decision ke beech mein interleave nahi kar sakta kyunki decision ek hi uninterrupted moment mein hoti hai.
how_it_works: rotating flag check karta hai, fail hone par throw, pass hone par pendingEntryOps increment karta hai -- dono steps synchronous hain.
in_this_project: manager.ts::claimEntryOp aur iska call addEntry, updateEntry, deleteEntry, getSharingPublicKey mein pehle await se pehle hota hai.
advantages: Prevents the add-vs-rotation race by construction, no mutex library needed
Fails fast with VAULT_BUSY instead of silently corrupting state
disadvantages: Every call site must remember to call this BEFORE any await, or the guarantee silently breaks
pendingEntryOps-- in the finally block must also never be forgotten, or the counter leaks forever
common_mistakes: Calling claimEntryOp() after an await by mistake, reopening the race window
Forgetting to decrement pendingEntryOps in a finally block, permanently blocking changeMasterPassword
follow_up_questions: What test in concurrency.test.ts illustrates the un-guarded version of this exact bug?
Why does changeMasterPassword check pendingEntryOps > 0 instead of calling claimEntryOp itself?
What would happen if claimEntryOp were called after the breach-check await instead of before?

question: Walk through requireSession(sessionId) line by line -- what three things can make it throw, and what does it do on success?
answer_hinglish: requireSession() har session-based call ka single choke point hai. Pehla check: const session = this.sessions.get(sessionId); if not session throw UNKNOWN_SESSION -- agar yeh sessionId kabhi issue hi nahi hua, ya lock() ho gaya tha, toh yahin reject. Doosra check: vault record nikalta hai aur record.generation not equal session.generation dekhta hai -- session apne unlock ke time ka generation capture karta hai, aur agar beech mein changeMasterPassword() ne vault ka generation bump kar diya hai, toh yeh mismatch ho jaata hai. Is case mein session ko sessions Map se DELETE karta hai, lazy cleanup, aur SESSION_INVALIDATED throw karta hai. Teesra check: clock.now() minus lastActivityAt greater than sessionIdleTimeoutMs -- agar session bahut der se idle hai, toh yeh bhi session ko delete karta hai aur SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT throw karta hai. Agar teeno check pass ho jaayein, toh last line hai: session.lastActivityAt = this.clock.now() -- matlab har SUCCESSFUL use session ke idle clock ko reset kar deta hai. Yahi wajah hai ki isSessionActive() alag function hai jo yahi generation and idle check karta hai par last line, reset, kabhi nahi karta -- warna sirf status poochna hi session ko zinda rakh deta, jo pura point defeat kar deta idle-timeout ka.
why_needed: Choke-point pattern samajhna zaroori hai kyunki yahi ek jagah hai jo poore session lifecycle ki correctness guarantee karti hai -- yahan ek bug har session-based call ko affect karega.
real_world_analogy: Ek office ka single turnstile gate jo badge check karta hai, expiry check karta hai, aur entry log karta hai -- agar koi doosra darwaza hota jo yeh checks skip kar deta, poora security model toot jaata.
how_it_works: Teen sequential checks: unknown session, generation mismatch, idle timeout -- fail hote hi throw, pass hone par lastActivityAt reset.
in_this_project: manager.ts::requireSession poore project mein har session-taking method (addEntry, getEntry, listEntries, updateEntry, deleteEntry, getSharingPublicKey, shareEntry, revokeShare, redeemShare) se call hota hai.
advantages: One choke point for both checking and resetting the idle clock -- no call site has to remember to do either
Lazy cleanup deletes dead sessions from the Map on their next failed use
disadvantages: A session that is never touched again after going idle stays in the sessions Map indefinitely until someone tries to use it
common_mistakes: Calling this from isSessionActive and accidentally resetting the idle clock, letting polling keep a session alive forever
Checking generation after checking idle timeout, which could report the wrong error code for a session that is both invalidated and idle
follow_up_questions: Why does isSessionActive duplicate some of this logic instead of calling requireSession?
What order are the three checks in, and does the order matter for which error code the caller sees?
How would you add metrics for how often SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT vs SESSION_INVALIDATED fires?

question: Walk through manager.ts's private commit() method -- what snapshot object does it build, and why are salt, canary, entries, sharingPublicKey and wrappedPrivateKey all passed in explicitly as a 'fields' argument instead of read directly off 'record'?
answer_hinglish: commit() ek private helper hai jo saari mutating operations, addEntry, updateEntry, deleteEntry, getSharingPublicKey, changeMasterPassword, use karti hain. Signature dekho: fields argument mein salt, canary, entries, sharingPublicKey, wrappedPrivateKey -- yeh explicit object parameter hai, record khud nahi. Function ke andar ek PersistedVault snapshot banta hai jo exactly yeh fields use karta hai, record se directly kuch nahi padhta, sirf ownerId aur createdAt, jo kabhi change nahi hote. Phir withTimeout se store.persist(snapshot, signal) call hota hai. Yeh explicit-fields pattern isliye hai ki COMMENT khud bolta hai: every field that can change is passed explicitly, never read implicitly off record, so a commit can never accidentally persist a stale salt or canary alongside a fresh set of entries, or vice versa. Socho changeMasterPassword() ka case: yeh NEW salt, canary, entries compute karta hai local variables mein, par record ke fields abhi tak PURANE hain, sirf commit succeed hone ke baad update hote hain. Agar commit() record.salt directly padhta, toh woh PURANA salt persist ho jaata jabki entries NAYE key se encrypted ja rahe hote -- exactly woh bug jo README ka S22 mutation check pakda tha. Explicit parameter passing yeh class of bug structurally impossible banata hai.
why_needed: Yeh ek concrete design decision hai jo ek real mutation-testing-discovered bug ko structurally impossible banata hai -- isse interview mein 'defensive API design' discuss kiya ja sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek cheque likhte waqt amount aur date hamesha explicitly likhna padta hai, system ki 'current date' se automatically nahi le sakte, warna ek delayed cheque galat date se clear ho sakta hai.
how_it_works: commit() fields object se snapshot banata hai, record se sirf immutable fields padhta hai, aur ek single store write karta hai.
in_this_project: manager.ts::commit sabhi mutating methods ke snapshot building ka single centralized point hai.
advantages: Structurally prevents stale-field bugs like S22
Every caller must think explicitly about what it is persisting
disadvantages: More verbose call sites -- every mutating method builds a full fields object
Does not prevent a caller from accidentally passing the wrong local variable, only prevents implicit staleness from record
common_mistakes: Reading record.salt inside commit() instead of fields.salt
Updating record's in-memory fields before commit() succeeds, breaking the 'nothing happens until the write succeeds' rule
follow_up_questions: What specific test closed the S22 gap, and what does it check that no earlier test did?
Why is ownerId and createdAt read from record but not salt, canary, or entries?
What would happen if two different mutating methods called commit() concurrently on the same record?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Explicit parameter passing thoda verbose hai -- har call site ko poora fields object banana padta hai, jabki record se directly padhna kam code hota. Par yeh verbosity ek real bug class ko compile-time-visible banati hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar commit() record se directly padhta aur koi caller record ko commit se PEHLE update kar deta, toh persisted snapshot aur actual commit intent mismatch ho jaata -- exactly S22 jaisa bug.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative hota record ko commit se pehle hi mutate karna aur phir commit() ko record se padhna -- par yeh commit succeed hone tak kuch apply nahi hota invariant tod deta, jo is poore project ka core design principle hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Yeh pattern scale-independent hai -- yeh ek correctness guarantee hai, performance se related nahi. Bade vaults par bhi yeh same explicit-fields discipline zaroori rehta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein ek typed test helper ban sakta hai jo HAR commit call ke baad store.lastPersisted() se directly compare kare live record se, jaise S22 ka fix tha, taaki yeh invariant continuously verified rahe.

question: Walk through sharing.ts's sealForRecipient and openAsRecipient -- what is oneTimeKey, what gets RSA-wrapped versus AES-encrypted, and what happens with a wrong recipient key?
answer_hinglish: sealForRecipient(recipientPublicKeyPem, plaintext) pehle randomBytes(32) se oneTimeKey banata hai -- ek fresh, random 256-bit AES key, SIRF is ek share ke liye, kahin stored nahi hoti. Phir encrypt(oneTimeKey, plaintext) -- yeh crypto.ts ka wahi AES-256-GCM function hai jo baaki poore project mein use hota hai, actual entry content title, username, password, notes isi oneTimeKey se encrypt hota hai. Phir publicEncrypt se sirf us CHHOTE oneTimeKey ko recipient ke RSA public key se wrap karta hai, RSA bade payloads encrypt nahi kar sakta, isliye sirf 32-byte key wrap hota hai, poora content nahi. Return hota hai wrappedKey aur blob -- yeh hybrid or envelope encryption hai, TLS or PGP jaisa pattern. openAsRecipient(recipientPrivateKeyPem, token) reverse karta hai: pehle privateDecrypt() se oneTimeKey nikalta hai apne private key se, phir decrypt(oneTimeKey, token.blob) se actual plaintext. Agar galat recipient ka private key use ho, ya wrappedKey corrupt ho, toh privateDecrypt() ek exception throw karta hai jo catch ho kar DECRYPTION_FAILED ban jaata hai, share token could not be unwrapped with this private key -- RSA yeh distinguish nahi karta ki galti kya thi, bilkul crypto.ts ke AES-GCM jaisa hi behavior.
why_needed: Hybrid encryption ek bahut common real-world pattern hai, TLS aur PGP dono use karte hain -- ise line by line samajhna crypto system design interviews ke liye bahut relevant hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhota safe-combination note (oneTimeKey) ko ek armored courier box mein daal kar RSA se lock karo -- asli saamaan (plaintext) itna bada hai ki armored box mein fit nahi hota, isliye woh alag se AES se encrypt hota hai.
how_it_works: Fresh AES key har share ke liye, content AES se encrypt, chhota key RSA se wrap, recipient apni private key se unwrap karta hai.
in_this_project: sharing.ts::sealForRecipient aur openAsRecipient manager.ts ke shareEntry aur redeemShare se call hote hain.
advantages: RSA only ever wraps a small, fixed-size key -- no payload-size limitation
Reuses crypto.ts's own AES-256-GCM for the actual content, no duplicated encryption logic
disadvantages: Two algorithms, RSA and AES, instead of one, slightly more surface area
RSA keypair generation, roughly 200ms, is comparatively expensive, hence the lazy, once-per-vault generation
common_mistakes: Trying to RSA-encrypt the entry content directly instead of wrapping a one-time AES key
Reusing the same oneTimeKey across multiple shares instead of generating a fresh one per sealForRecipient call
follow_up_questions: Why is a fresh oneTimeKey generated per share instead of reusing the vault's own key?
What test in sharing.test.ts proves the same plaintext sealed twice never produces the same token?
Why does an invalid recipient public key get INVALID_REQUEST while a wrong private key gets DECRYPTION_FAILED?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Hybrid encryption RSA ki speed and size limitation ko bypass karta hai -- sirf 32 bytes RSA se wrap hote hain, baaki sab fast AES se. Trade-off yeh hai ki do algorithms manage karne padte hain ek ki jagah, par yeh industry-standard pattern hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi wrong recipient ka token redeem karne ki koshish kare, privateDecrypt() fail hoga aur DECRYPTION_FAILED throw hoga -- manager.ts ka redeemShare() iss case mein share ka claim release kar deta hai, taaki real recipient abhi bhi apna valid attempt kar sake.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative hota ECIES, elliptic curve based envelope encryption, jo chhota aur faster hota, par README explicitly bolta hai RSA-OAEP chosen hua kyunki Node ka publicEncrypt and privateDecrypt directly support karta hai bina extra key-derivation logic likhne ke.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x scale par har naya share ek fresh RSA-OAEP operation hai jo CPU-heavy hai compared to pure AES -- agar sharing bahut high-frequency feature ban jaaye, toh RSA operations ek bottleneck ban sakte hain.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein key size, abhi 2048-bit, periodically review karna chahiye crypto best-practices ke against, aur agar sharing volume bahut high ho jaaye, ECC-based hybrid scheme ki migration consider karni chahiye.

question: Walk through timeout.ts's withTimeout -- how do the AbortController and timedOut flag work together, how does manager.ts's commit() use it, and what was the actual W3 mutation bug it exposed?
answer_hinglish: withTimeout(run, timeoutMs) ek generic helper hai jo kisi bhi async function ko ek deadline ke against race karta hai. Pehle AbortController banta hai aur timedOut false set hota hai. Phir setTimeout schedule hota hai jo agar deadline tak pahunche, timedOut ko true karta hai AUR controller.abort() call karta hai, jisse controller.signal ko pass kiya gaya koi bhi well-behaved async function apna kaam rok sakta hai. try block mein await run(controller.signal) -- caller ka actual function chalta hai, signal milta hai. Agar yeh reject ho, chahe genuine error ho ya abort ki wajah se, catch block check karta hai if timedOut throw STORE_TIMEOUT -- matlab agar timer already fire ho chuka tha jab failure aayi, specific STORE_TIMEOUT error throw hota hai; warna original error wapas throw hota hai. SABSE IMPORTANT LINE: finally clearTimeout(timer) -- yeh guarantee karta hai ki agar run() SUCCESSFULLY resolve ho jaaye, deadline se pehle, toh bhi timer clear ho. manager.ts ka commit() isko exactly aise use karta hai, await withTimeout call ke andar store.persist. README ka mutation W3 exactly is finally block ko target karta hai: a successful commit never called clearTimeout on its deadline timer -- is bug mein, har successful, non-timing-out, commit bhi apna setTimeout timer kabhi clear nahi karta tha, jo memory mein hamesha ke liye lingering timers accumulate karta, ek real production memory or resource leak, jo vi.getTimerCount() check se catch hua.
why_needed: Timeout aur resource cleanup patterns har distributed system mein zaroori hain -- ek missed clearTimeout jaisa chhota bug production mein slow memory leak ban sakta hai, isliye yeh line-by-line samajhna important hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek alarm clock set karna 'agar main 10 minute mein na uthoon toh bell bajao' -- agar tum khud uth jaate ho time se pehle, toh alarm ko manually off karna zaroori hai, warna woh baad mein bajegi hi, resource waste karega.
how_it_works: AbortController plus setTimeout cooperative cancellation deta hai; finally block hamesha timer clear karta hai, success ya failure dono mein.
in_this_project: timeout.ts::withTimeout manager.ts::commit mein store.persist ko wrap karta hai; README ka W3 mutation isi finally block ko remove karke test karta hai.
advantages: Cooperative cancellation via AbortSignal lets a well-behaved store stop its own work
The finally block guarantees timer cleanup on both success and failure paths
disadvantages: Relies on the wrapped function actually checking signal.aborted -- InMemoryVaultStore does check it, but a badly-written store would not actually stop
common_mistakes: Forgetting clearTimeout in the finally block, as the W3 mutation check found, leaking a timer on every successful call
Checking timedOut before the setTimeout callback has had a chance to run, causing a race in tests without fake timers
follow_up_questions: How does InMemoryVaultStore.persist use the signal it receives?
Why check timedOut instead of directly checking controller.signal.aborted in the catch block?
What test under fake timers specifically proves a successful commit clears its timer?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: AbortSignal-based racing ek clean idiom hai jo cooperative cancellation deta hai, par yeh assume karta hai ki run() signal ko respect karega -- agar koi badly-behaved store implementation signal ignore kare, toh underlying operation abhi bhi background mein chalta rahega.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar finally block ka clearTimeout() na hota, jaise W3 mutation, toh har successful commit bhi apna timer leave kar deta -- high-throughput system mein yeh timers accumulate ho kar memory leak ban jaata.
advanced.alternatives: Ek alternative hota Promise.race ke saath ek timeout promise, bina AbortSignal ke -- par woh underlying operation ko actually cancel karne ka koi tareeka nahi deta, sirf caller ko early return deta while real work background mein chalta rehta.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x scale par bahut zyada concurrent commits ho sakte hain -- agar clearTimeout() miss ho, jaisa W3 tha, toh timers ki sheer volume Node ke event loop ko measurably slow kar sakti hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Production mein timer count ya pending-abort-controller count ko metric ke roop mein expose karna useful hota, taaki aisa leak production mein turant dikhe, jaisa yahan vi.getTimerCount() test mein hua tha.
